tagline.text: A Marinduque limestone cave with an underground river and waterfall in Santa Cruz

location.label: Location
location.text: Santa Cruz, Marinduque — a limestone cave running from the San Isidro entrance to the Punong exit

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (per person, inland transport and cave fees on Marinduque; Manila round-trip transport excluded)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Marinduque Airport (MRQ, no scheduled flights) — most travelers come overland and by ferry from Manila

children.text: Bagumbungan Cave is a limestone cave about 1.9 km long in Santa Cruz, Marinduque, and the island's best-known caving trip, with stalactites, stalagmites, an underground river and a waterfall. A guide is required, and you can choose a short route to the falls or the full traverse to the Punong exit.
Bagumbungan Cave lies in the municipality of Santa Cruz on Marinduque. It is a limestone cave passage about
1.9km

long that begins at an entrance on the San Isidro side and comes out at an exit on the Punong side. It is also called San Isidro Cave, and the entrance is said to be near Sitio Puti. Stalactites, stalagmites, limestone columns, an underground river and a waterfall inside the cave follow one another, and it is regarded as the island's best-known caving destination. Marinduque is better known for the Moriones Festival and quiet island villages than for resort beaches, so this cave is a distinctive choice for travelers who want something physical.

The cave became known only recently. According to a government blog post, a provincial tourism office team and cave enthusiasts from Santa Cruz found it in 2009, and its underground river became known. Another account says local residents first came across it while gathering swiftlet nests, and that after a caver alerted the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the passages and wildlife were surveyed and mapped. It is said to have opened to visitors around 2013, so it is still a fairly young attraction of a little over ten years.

In 2012 the cave was added to the DENR list of protected caves. Under the National Caves and Cave Resources Management and Protection Act (Republic Act No. 9072), DENR Memorandum Circular 2012-03 designated 158 caves nationwide as protected, and Bagumbungan is classified as Class II, meaning a cave with both hazardous conditions and sensitive geological, biological or cultural value. Parts of a Class II cave may be closed seasonally or permanently, and in practice some sections here are off-limits for safety. The aim is to protect the cave from treasure hunters and vandals, so visitors should respect the rules.

It helps to know what kind of experience this is. It is not a lit tourist walkway but real caving: you wear a helmet and headlamp and move through mud and water. Visitors commonly mention squeezing through narrow gaps, climbing over boulders and columns, wading through water that reaches waist to hip height, and a section of complete darkness without light. Beginners are said to be able to do it with a guide, but be ready to get wet and dirty, and think carefully if you are claustrophobic. Getting here from Manila takes close to a full day by bus and ferry, so plan to set aside half a day of your Marinduque trip for the cave. This guide is for travelers who want to fit Bagumbungan Cave into a Marinduque trip. Fees, operating hours and routes differ slightly between sources, so only figures that several sources agree on are given, and the rest is left as "check locally." Before you go, ask the Santa Cruz local government (LGU) tourism office or the cave registration hall about the latest operating status.
The main attraction is the route through the cave from the San Isidro entrance to the Punong exit. The full route is described as a passage of about
1.9km
, and coming out in a different village after passing through the whole cave is what sets it apart from an ordinary cave visit.

Limestone formations built up over thousands of years, including stalactites, stalagmites, flowstones and rimstones, follow one another. Visitors have also reported formations that look like an eagle, an angel or a mermaid's tail, so ask your guide to point them out for extra fun.

An underground river flows through the cave and there is a waterfall. The short route ends at this waterfall, and some stretches require wading through water at waist or hip height, so be ready to get wet.

There is said to be a section with no light at all once your headlamp is off. Many visitors say that switching off lights for a moment at the guide's instruction and feeling the darkness and the sound of dripping water is memorable. Never do this on your own.

There is a section with bats, and visitor accounts mention shrimp, crabs, eels, catfish and even an owl. The cave is protected, so look but do not touch, and follow the guide's instructions about using flash.

You can choose a short route to the falls or the full route to the Punong exit. Many visitors recommend the full route if you have the energy and time, and it is described as taking roughly 3 to 4 hours including rests.

The cave is managed by village residents and the local government under DENR protection, and trained local guide groups lead the trips. The fee is said to include the environmental fee, entrance fee, guide and equipment rental, so travelers need to bring little gear of their own.

Because it opened to tourism only recently, you can enjoy the cave in a calmer setting than at big tourist sites. Group visits can still overlap, so check locally before you go. Inside the cave, move slowly at the guide's pace and take photos only from safe spots.

At the cave registration hall, register, pay the fees and attend the guide's safety orientation. You will be given a helmet, headlamp and gloves. The hall is said to have restrooms where you can change.
Enter the cave with your guide, pass the falls and walk through to the Punong exit. Including photos and rests, it usually takes around
3–4 hours
Come out of the exit into the village and change out of your wet clothes. If you did not arrange lunch, you will rely on snacks and water, so pack them before you set out.
Take a tricycle to Lamesa, then a jeepney back to Boac. The last trips leave early, so check locally.

children.text: From central Santa Cruz, take a jeepney or tricycle toward the Bagumbungan area.
After registration and orientation, go in as far as the waterfall. The fee is about
, half the full-route price.
Return the way you came, then wash and change. In the rest of the afternoon you can look around Santa Cruz, for example Holy Cross Parish.
The short route returns through the same passage, so you do not experience the full traverse to the Punong exit.

items.title: From Manila by bus and ferry

children.text: In Manila, take a bus to Lucena, for example JAC Liner from Cubao. The air-conditioned fare is about
and the trip takes
3–5 hours
. Most buses stop at the Lucena Grand Terminal, and a tricycle from there to Dalahican Wharf costs about
and takes
10–15 minutes
From Dalahican, take a Starhorse or Montenegro ferry to Balanacan port in Mogpog. The crossing takes
3–4 hours
, and the Starhorse adult fare is about
under its October 2026 rate sheet (students and seniors get discounts). Lucena departures run about six times a day from 2:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m., but times change without notice, so check.
From Balanacan to Santa Cruz, a jeepney or van takes about
30 minutes to a little over an hour
and costs about
, according to guides. From Santa Cruz, reach the cave village by the jeepney and tricycle connections described in the itinerary above.
A direct bus from Cubao to Santa Cruz (including the ferry) is reported to run on Monday, Wednesday and Friday afternoons. The fare is reported at about
, so confirm it when you book.
To reach Marinduque from Manila in one day, match an early bus with a morning ferry. Routes and fares changed several times even during 2026, so check just before you leave.

Marinduque Airport (MRQ) is in Gasan. As of 2026 it is reported to have no scheduled commercial flights and to handle only general aviation such as small charters. The last scheduled Manila–Gasan flight is said to have been in April 2023, so do not rely on flight information in older travel posts.
From Boac, take a jeepney toward Santa Cruz via Lamesa to San Isidro. From central Santa Cruz, you can reach the cave village by jeepney or tricycle.
If you charter a tricycle, the price is negotiable, and return transport stops early in the afternoon, so ask the driver to wait or agree on a return time in advance.

The dry season from November to May is the best time for the cave. Some sources put the dry season at December to May, so check the weather just before you go. In the dry season the water in the cave is lower and the passages are less dangerous, so the waterfall and underground river sections can be crossed more safely.

In rainy periods the cave can flood, and July and August are said to be especially dangerous. If there has been heavy rain recently, follow your guide's judgment, and accept that being refused entry is a safety measure. Starting in the morning also lowers the risk of late-afternoon showers.

The cave village has little information on tourist lodging or restaurants, so most visitors stay in Santa Cruz town or Boac and visit as a day trip. Lodgings listed in Santa Cruz include Villa d' Arco Resort, Jethro Hotel and Resto and Cavesera Residencia. Boac has larger lodgings and is convenient for a first night after arriving from Manila.

There is no store in the cave, so bring water, snacks and cash. Groups of 10 or more can reserve a local kamayan lunch (a Filipino spread eaten by hand) in advance. Individual travelers eat lunch or dinner at restaurants in Santa Cruz town.
A guide is required. Register at the local registration hall and be assigned a guide, and never enter alone.
Wear clothes you do not mind getting wet and muddy, and shoes with good grip (water shoes or trekking shoes). Sandals are not suitable.
A helmet and headlamp are described as included in the fee, but bringing a spare headlamp and batteries is reassuring.
Put your phone, wallet and camera in a waterproof bag or dry bag. The water can reach waist height.
Pack a towel and a change of clothes separately for the exit. The registration hall is said to have restrooms for changing.
Bring plenty of cash. There is no ATM near the cave village, and guide and village fees are paid in cash.
Start early in the morning. Public transport back is reported to stop in the early afternoon.
Before you go, ask the Santa Cruz local government tourism office or the cave contact (listed as 0916 750 1442) whether the cave is operating.
In rainy periods the cave can flood and become dangerous, so always follow your guide if they close it.
This is a DENR-designated Class II protected cave, and some sections are closed. Do not enter any place your guide forbids.
Some passages are narrow and slippery, so there is a risk of injury. If you have severe claustrophobia or a heart condition, are pregnant or have bad joints, think carefully before taking part.
Do not touch or break stalactites and stalagmites. Take your trash with you, and do not make noise or shine lights at animals such as bats and swiftlets.
Fees, operating hours and transport differ between sources. Check the latest announcements for the figures in this guide.

In an emergency, call the Philippine emergency number 911 or the Santa Cruz disaster response office (listed as 0920-455-4034). Phones may not work inside the cave, so agree on a way to communicate with your guide before you set out.

The center of Marinduque, with a Spanish-era cathedral and historic sites. It has many lodgings and restaurants, making it a good base for travelers arriving from Manila, and you reach the cave from here by jeepney via Lamesa.
For the island's other sights and Moriones Festival information, see the Marinduque guide as well.
Reached by outrigger boat from Buyabod port in Santa Cruz. Island-hopping stops include the Palad sandbar (visible only at low tide) and the Ungab rock arch.
Bathala Caves are in the village of Ipil, and Kawa-Kawa Falls are in the village of Bangcuangan. Water volume at the falls is high just after the rains, so go with a guide if it is your first time.
A parish said to have been built in 1714, within walking distance of Santa Cruz town plaza.
